Subject: Post-demo: reliability & SLO competitive checklist + proposed tests

Hi Alice —

Thanks again for taking the time this morning. I pulled together a short recap of the reliability and SLO topics we discussed plus a proposed set of hands-on tests so CloudCorp can validate differences between Redwood and the hyperscaler endpoints you’re evaluating. High-level notes first, then concrete next steps.

Key differentiators (quick):
- Deterministic routing and model fallback: we can pin a primary model and configure an automatic fallback to a lower-cost variant in the same API surface when capacity or error thresholds are hit. Hyperscalers often require separate endpoints for different variants, which complicates failover.
- Error budget controls exposed to customers: you get per-route error budgets and automatic throttling policies you can tune.
- Prefix/KV caching for session workloads: reduces per-token cost and lowers 99th percentile latency for chat-style sessions.
- Observable SLIs out of the box: token-level latency distribution, error-class breakdowns, and per-token cost — all exportable to your monitoring.

Reliability & SLO comparison (summary):
- Uptime target: Redwood hosted SLOs (standard) = 99.95% monthly; enterprise Dedicated SLA can be 99.99% with reserved pools. Hyperscalers typically offer 99.95% for managed model inference; implementation differences and regional redundancy vary.
- Rate limits: Redwood default API rate is per-account with burst buckets and configurable per-route caps; can be bumped for Dedicated plans. Hyperscalers impose fixed regional rate limits per endpoint that are harder to change at short notice.
- Error budgets & graceful degradation: Redwood supports soft-fail policies (return cached prefix or reduced-length completions) + model fallback; many hyperscaler setups return 5xx or block requests unless you build an additional layer.
- Failover behavior: Redwood has multi-region routing + automatic model variant fallback. Hyperscalers rely on regional failover but often require separate configuration for model versions.

Proposed empirical tests (we recommend running these in parallel against both Redwood and your hyperscaler candidate):
1) Sustained 90th/95th/99th load run (48 hours): ramp to expected peak TPS and hold. Measure 99th latency, tail spikes, and any error rate increases.
2) Burst/spike test: short ramp to 5x peak for 10 minutes to validate burst policies and throttling behavior.
3) Cold-start & eviction test: idle a model pool and then drive traffic to measure first-request latency and KV cache warmup behavior.
4) Failover simulation: induce a synthetic 10% region outage (via our fault injector) and validate: routing, model fallback, and client-visible errors.
5) Error-budget enforcement: create a synthetic error class (e.g., transient GPU OOM) and verify soft-fail vs hard 5xx behaviors.

Attachments: included is a compact reliability matrix and a sample benchmark log export (stubs attached).

Next steps I propose:
- If this looks good, we schedule a 90-minute benchmark kickoff for next Wednesday (Mar 10). Redwood will provision a temporary dedicated pool (2x your expected baseline) for a 72-hour run and we’ll share a prebuilt k6 scenario.
- Rishi will share the routing/ARNs and the temporary API key; Neha will own the test harness integration and metrics export.
- You loop in your security team if they want a short checklist; I attached the minimal SOC/attestation references so your Security can triage quickly.

Can you confirm the kickoff window and whether you want the Dedicated trial or a hosted run first?

Best,

—

Marissa —

Thanks for the clear summary. A few clarifying questions from my side before we lock the kickoff:
1) For the 99.95 vs 99.99 messaging — is the 99.99 SLA only available on Dedicated contracts? What does the standard SLA cover for hosted accounts beyond 99.95?
2) For model fallback: can you confirm the semantics? If the primary model returns 5xx, do you automatically retry on a fallback model and surface the fallback response to the client with a header indicating fallback used?
3) For the rate limits — if we hit the per-route cap during a spike, what is the default behavior? Queue? 429? Throttle?

On security: they want the SOC reference but are also asking for any past incidents where a customer saw meaningful availability degradation and how Redwood handled the postmortem and remediation steps.

We prefer to run the Hosted trial first (lower friction) unless Dedicated is necessary to reproduce the exact SLA behavior. Kickoff window next Wed (Mar 10) works for us in the morning PST.

Thanks,
Alice

Hi Alice — answers inline below and added some test-implementation notes.

1) SLA tiers: correct — 99.99% is available as part of our Dedicated reserved-capacity contracts where we provision isolated GPU pools and an SLA commitment in the contract. Hosted customers get a standard SLO of 99.95% with an uptime credit policy (details attached). The difference isn’t just the number: Dedicated pools provide capacity isolation which reduces noisy-neighbor risk and allows us to guarantee lower tail latency under your committed throughput. We can provision a temporary Dedicated pool for the trial if you want exact parity with production assumptions.

2) Model fallback semantics: by default we implement a single automatic retry on a compatible variant with the following behavior:
   - If primary returns transient 5xx or we detect high token failure rates, we dispatch a single retry to the configured fallback model.
   - The client receives the fallback response with an X-Redwood-Fallback header and a metadata block in the response containing the fallback model id and the reason (e.g., PRIMARY_5XX, TIMEOUT).
   - Retries are rate-limited and bounded (1 retry by default) to avoid thundering herd. This is configurable per-route.

3) Rate-limit behavior: default behavior is to return a 429 with a Retry-After header when a hard per-account per-route cap is reached. We also support a queueing mode for Dedicated customers where short bursts are queued for up to 10s (configurable) before returning 429s. For your tests, we’ll enable the queueing mode on the temporary trial pool so you can observe the queued latency vs immediate 429 behavior.

Security/incidents: public incident history is limited; we do surface postmortems for any incident that triggers a customer-visible SLO miss. I attached a redacted postmortem for a 2024 regional networking incident which shows timeline, root cause (edge-router config regression), mitigations (automated canary rollout guards), and compensating controls we added (improved health-checks and expanded cross-region routing). If your security team needs, we can schedule a 30-minute review with our Security / Reliability leads and share a tighter redaction that has sensitive internal IDs removed.

Implementation notes for the tests:
- I will share a k6 scenario with the 48-hour and spike workloads. Neha will produce a Prometheus/OTel exporter we can point at your metrics collector and also push a copy to the shared drive.
- We’ll tag all trial traffic with a test-id header (X-Redwood-Test-Id) so we can slice the logs and produce a side-by-side reliability matrix post-run.

I’ll start the trial provisioning once you confirm Hosted vs Dedicated. I recommend Hosted first (as you suggested) and then a short Dedicated run if we see behavior that requires capacity isolation.

Proposed kickoff: Wed, Mar 10, 09:00 PT — 90 minutes. Confirm and I’ll send a calendar invite with pre-reqs.

Best,
Marissa
